introduction_markdown:
This paper is arranged in three sections, A, B and C. Section A: answer ALL 5 questions; you will be graded for the best 4 answers. Section B: answer ALL 2 questions in this section using the spaces provided; both questions carry equal marks. Section C: answer ONLY TWO questions out of three; if you attempt more than 2 questions, only the first two will be considered. Where appropriate, equations and diagrams should be used to illustrate your answers. In calculations, you are advised to show all the steps in your working, giving your answer at each stage. Calculators are allowed. You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

**Useful data:** specific heat capacity of water = 4.2 J g$^{-1}$ $^\circ$C$^{-1}$; 1 faraday = 96000 coulombs; Avogadro number = $6.02\times10^{23}$; molar volume of a gas at r.t.p. = 24000 cm$^3$.

You are provided with the following requirements: Beaker, pipette, 250 cm$^3$ volumetric flask, burette, conical flask, anhydrous sodium carbonate, wash bottle, dilute sulphuric acid, distilled water, phenolphthalein indicator.

You are required to prepare 250 cm$^3$ of $0.1\,\mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{Na_2CO_3(aq)}$ and use this standard solution to determine the concentration of dilute sulphuric acid.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Outline 3 key steps to prepare the standard solution. *[3 marks]*

(ii) State one precaution in preparing the standard solution. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) Three key steps:

1. **Weigh** accurately the calculated mass of anhydrous sodium carbonate (2.65 g, see (b)) and **dissolve** it in a little distilled water in a clean beaker, stirring until it has all dissolved.
2. **Transfer** the solution into the 250 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask, then rinse the beaker (and stirring rod) with distilled water from the wash bottle and add the washings to the flask so that no solute is lost.
3. Add distilled water until the level is close to the mark, then add the last drops with the wash bottle until the **bottom of the meniscus rests on the mark**; stopper the flask and **invert it several times** to mix thoroughly.

(ii) One precaution (any one): add the washings of the beaker to the flask so that no sodium carbonate is lost; do not go above the graduation mark (read the meniscus at eye level); mix well before use; use distilled water only; weigh the anhydrous sodium carbonate quickly and keep its bottle closed because it absorbs moisture from the air.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Identify the main apparatus in which you would prepare the standard solution.

(ii) Calculate the mass of solid sodium carbonate that you would use to prepare the $0.1\,\mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{Na_2CO_3(aq)}$. (Molar mass of sodium carbonate is 106 g/mol) *[3 marks]*

(iii) Suggest a piece of equipment, not given above, that is used to weigh the solid sodium carbonate. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) The **250 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ volumetric flask**.

(ii) Amount of sodium carbonate needed:

$$
n = c \times V = 0.1\ \mathrm{mol\,dm^{-3}} \times \frac{250}{1000}\ \mathrm{dm^3} = 0.025\ \mathrm{mol}
$$

Mass:

$$
m = n \times M = 0.025\ \mathrm{mol} \times 106\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}} = 2.65\ \mathrm{g}
$$

The mass of sodium carbonate required is **2.65 g**.

(iii) A **(top-pan or electronic) balance**, also called a weighing balance.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(i) Name the technique used to determine the concentration of dilute sulphuric acid using the standard solution.

(ii) Explain why it is better to place the dilute sulphuric acid in the burette.

(iii) Suggest an appropriate cleaning procedure for the

Burette: ........

Pipette: ........ *[4 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i) **Titration** (an acid-base titration).

(ii) Sodium carbonate solution is **alkaline**, and alkalis attack glass, so a burette containing it can have its glass tap or stopcock stick or jam. The dilute acid does not damage the glass, so it is placed in the burette and run slowly into the **measured 25 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ of sodium carbonate** in the conical flask, which makes the end point (colour change of the indicator) easy to see and the volume added easy to read.

(iii) Cleaning procedure:

- **Burette:** rinse with **distilled water**, then rinse with a small volume of the **dilute sulphuric acid** that it will contain (so that water left on the glass does not dilute the acid).
- **Pipette:** rinse with **distilled water**, then rinse with a little of the **sodium carbonate solution** that it will deliver.

questions.enonce_markdown:
In an experiment to determine the concentration of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$ using $0.1\,\mathrm{M}\ \mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$, 25 cm$^3$ of $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3(aq)}$ exactly neutralized 20 cm$^3$ of dilute $\mathrm{H_2SO_4(aq)}$.

The reaction is $\mathrm{H_2SO_4 + Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow Na_2SO_4 + CO_2 + H_2O}$

(i) Determine the concentration of the acid in $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$ *[3 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
Amount of sodium carbonate used:

$$
n(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}) = 0.1 \times \frac{25}{1000} = 0.0025\ \mathrm{mol}
$$

From the equation, 1 mol of $\mathrm{Na_2CO_3}$ reacts with 1 mol of $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$, so $n(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = 0.0025\ \mathrm{mol}$. This amount is contained in 20 $\mathrm{cm^3}$ $= 0.020\ \mathrm{dm^3}$ of acid:

$$
c(\mathrm{H_2SO_4}) = \frac{0.0025}{0.020} = 0.125\ \mathrm{mol/dm^3}
$$

The concentration of the sulphuric acid is **0.125 $\mathrm{mol/dm^3}$**.

questions.enonce_markdown:
Sublimation, use of a separating funnel, evaporation to dryness, fractional distillation, filtration and crystallization are techniques used to separate mixtures.

(i) Choose the most suitable technique to separate;

Salt from sea water: ........

Silver chloride from its mixture with water: ........

Water from kerosene: ........ *[3 marks]*

(ii) State the property of water and kerosene that enables them to be separated by the method in (e)iii above. *[1 mark]*

(iii) Give an example of a mixture that can be separated by chromatography. *[1 mark]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
(i)

| Mixture | Technique |
|---|---|
| Salt from sea water | **Evaporation to dryness** (the water evaporates and the salt is left behind) |
| Silver chloride from its mixture with water | **Filtration** (silver chloride is insoluble and stays on the filter paper) |
| Water from kerosene | **Separating funnel** |

(ii) Water and kerosene are **immiscible**: they do not mix and form two separate layers (water, the denser liquid, is below). The lower layer is run off through the tap of the separating funnel.

(iii) A mixture of **coloured dyes** (for example the dyes in black ink or the pigments of a leaf extract) can be separated by paper chromatography.
